## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{100}{0}{0}{0}{0}{0}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why can a model with a tenth of the token price make an agent cost more for every task it finishes?_

A team that prices an agent from its token bill misses much of what it buys. Each accepted result carries model calls, sandbox time, tool fees, assessment, and any human work, together with the spending on tasks that never passed. A cheaper model can require more turns and leave more work unresolved; a faster model barely shortens a trajectory whose time goes to tests and tool waits. Economics therefore connects model choice, caching, reasoning budgets, routing, and capacity to the outcome the service is meant to deliver. Lower cost matters within declared acceptance and deadline constraints, and a deadline benefit can justify higher spending. Horizon sets how many steps require funding, state affects what each step must retain and read, and authority determines which effects need mediation and assessment, making the cost of closure a property of the whole trajectory.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Calculate cohort cost per accepted task while distinguishing attempt costs, human outcomes, and unsettled liabilities
- Evaluate caching, compaction, and reasoning or retry purchases under explicit billing and acceptance assumptions
- Diagnose critical-path investments using execution dependencies, component costs, and available serving capacity
- Evaluate model cascades under a common acceptance contract, including assessment costs and false-accept risk
- Size resource occupancy and compare provisioning choices under declared workload, quota, and queueing assumptions
- Design atomic budget reservations that preserve spending bounds across concurrent work and late settlement
- Select an architecture using declared acceptance, cost, latency, and authority constraints rather than agent count

:::

## Cost per Accepted Task {#sec-vol3-agent-economics-accounting}

A bug-fixing service can spend less on each model call and more on each accepted repair. The cheaper calls may require additional turns, each holding a sandbox and invoking tools, and more tickets may remain unresolved after assessment. The token discount is real, but it applies to only part of the account. The engineering comparison must join spending to the same task outcomes whose evidence the evaluation chapter established.

Acceptance remains scoped to a declared contract, checker, and environment. A passing regression suite is evidence for the properties it checks, not an observation that the patch has no latent defects. Changing that contract while changing models would confound the economic comparison. The account also needs a population and a cutoff: which initiated tasks it covers, which results were accepted by the cutoff, and which operations, assessments, or charges remain pending.

### From an attempt to a task account

Across an attempt of $K$ turns, the runtime incurs model charges and pays for the environment in which proposed actions execute. Assessment, cleanup, and human work may continue after the final model call. A useful decomposition is

$$C_{\text{attempt}} = \sum_{k=1}^K \left(C_{\text{in},k}+C_{\text{out},k}+C_{\text{tools},k}+C_{\text{sandbox},k}\right)+C_{\text{verify}}+C_{\text{cleanup}}+C_{\text{human}}+C_{\text{runtime}}.$$

The input and output terms use the applicable billing categories, including any cached-input charges. The tool term covers external service fees; the sandbox term covers its charged lifetime, including waits when the resource remains allocated. Verification covers assessment not already charged elsewhere. Cleanup includes required release or compensation work, and the human term includes the declared review or handling boundary. Runtime cost includes orchestration and allocated shared infrastructure overhead. Each charge belongs in exactly one category: a test billed as sandbox execution must not also appear as a second verification charge for that same resource.

::: {#dfn-whole-trajectory-cost .callout-definition title="Whole-trajectory cost"}

***Whole-trajectory cost***\index{Whole-trajectory cost!definition} is the total cost attributed to one execution attempt across its model calls, environment, assessment, and required finalization within a declared accounting boundary.

1. **Significance**: It exposes costs that a per-token price omits, including work on attempts that never produce an accepted result.
2. **Distinction**: It prices an attempt. Cost per accepted task also includes spending on other attempts and tasks in the counted population.
3. **Common pitfall**: Ending the account when a local agent stops even though remote operations, cleanup, or human handling still incur charges.

:::

An initiated task can contain several attempts or delegated branches. Its task account, $C_{\text{task},i}$, includes all of that work once, together with the task's share of capacity and operations costs. A failed or canceled branch does not disappear from the account because its output was discarded. A reserved amount is not yet an actual charge; it backs authorized work or possible liability and cannot be released while the obligations it covers remain unresolved. Reports at an intermediate cutoff therefore distinguish settled spending from outstanding liabilities; they do not report the settled subtotal as the final price of the task.

### Charging all work to accepted outcomes

For a finite cohort of $N$ initiated tasks with completed accounting, let $N_{\text{acc}}$ be the number of distinct tasks accepted under the declared contract. Repeated successful attempts at the same task do not create additional accepted tasks. For $N_{\text{acc}}>0$,

$$C_{\text{eff}}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}C_{\text{task},i}}{N_{\text{acc}}}. $$

This is cost per accepted task. The numerator includes every initiated task, not just the accepted ones. If none is accepted, no finite cost-per-accepted ratio exists; report the spending and zero accepted outcomes directly. When outcomes or charges are pending, report those statuses and the cutoff alongside any provisional ratio. A missing assessment is not automatically a failed assessment, and a late charge can change the ratio without changing the artifact.

For a fully classified cohort, write $\alpha=N_{\text{acc}}/N$. Let $C_{\text{succ}}$ be the mean total task cost among accepted tasks and $C_{\text{fail}}$ the mean among nonaccepted tasks, including failed and canceled tasks. When both groups are nonempty, separating the numerator gives

$$C_{\text{eff}}=C_{\text{succ}}+\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}C_{\text{fail}}.$$

The multiplier $(1-\alpha)/\alpha$ counts nonaccepted tasks per accepted task. It is a cohort identity, not an assumption that independent retries eventually solve every ticket. Its economic effect depends on both groups' costs. There is no universal acceptance-rate threshold below which a token discount must lose: a sufficiently cheap policy can remain cheaper despite lower acceptance, while a modest discount can fail to compensate for expensive unsuccessful work. Acceptance coverage and deadlines still constrain which policy is useful.

The bug-repair calculation below retains that distinction by assigning one bounded attempt to each ticket. Its human charge is triage of rejected attempts, not a claim that an engineer subsequently resolves them.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-agent-economics-token-price
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE TOKEN-PRICE FALLACY IN A FINITE BUG-REPAIR COHORT (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Goal: Compare total spend per accepted task, with and without human triage.
# │ Show: Model and attempt costs, cohort costs, and accepted-task ratios.
# │ How:  One bounded attempt per ticket; all outcomes and charges settled.
# │ Note: Hypothetical prices and counts, not a provider schedule or experiment.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_usd, fmt_int, fmt_multiple

class TokenPriceFallacy:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    tickets = 100
    a_accepted, b_accepted = 75, 25
    a_in, a_out = 3.00, 15.00  # scenario USD per million tokens
    b_in, b_out = 0.30, 1.20
    a_turns, b_turns = 4, 7
    a_ctx, a_gen = 16_000, 800  # scenario tokens per turn
    b_ctx, b_gen = 28_000, 1_200
    c_env = 0.03  # scenario USD per turn, all tool/sandbox holding charges
    c_verify = 0.05  # scenario USD per attempt, additional assessment
    c_human = 10.00  # scenario USD per rejected attempt, triage only

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    a_model = a_turns * (a_ctx * a_in + a_gen * a_out) / 1e6
    b_model = b_turns * (b_ctx * b_in + b_gen * b_out) / 1e6
    a_attempt = a_model + a_turns * c_env + c_verify
    b_attempt = b_model + b_turns * c_env + c_verify
    a_total, b_total = tickets * a_attempt, tickets * b_attempt
    a_rejected, b_rejected = tickets - a_accepted, tickets - b_accepted
    a_total_h = a_total + a_rejected * c_human
    b_total_h = b_total + b_rejected * c_human
    a_eff, b_eff = a_total / a_accepted, b_total / b_accepted
    a_eff_h, b_eff_h = a_total_h / a_accepted, b_total_h / b_accepted
    eff_ratio, eff_h_ratio = b_eff / a_eff, b_eff_h / a_eff_h

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0 < b_accepted < a_accepted < tickets, "Both cohorts need accepted and rejected tasks")
    check(a_accepted + a_rejected == tickets and b_accepted + b_rejected == tickets, "Every initiated ticket must have a declared outcome")
    check(b_model < a_model and b_attempt < a_attempt, "Cheap model must cost less per attempt")
    check(b_eff > a_eff and eff_h_ratio > eff_ratio, "Acceptance and triage reverse the ranking")
    check(abs(a_total_h - a_total - a_rejected * c_human) < 1e-9, "Triage cost must be included exactly once")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    tickets_str = fmt_int(tickets)
    a_accepted_str, b_accepted_str = fmt_int(a_accepted), fmt_int(b_accepted)
    a_rejected_str, b_rejected_str = fmt_int(a_rejected), fmt_int(b_rejected)
    a_in_str, a_out_str = fmt_usd(a_in, precision=0), fmt_usd(a_out, precision=0)
    b_in_str, b_out_str = fmt_usd(b_in, precision=2), fmt_usd(b_out, precision=2)
    a_turns_str, b_turns_str = fmt_int(a_turns), fmt_int(b_turns)
    a_ctx_str, a_gen_str = fmt_int(a_ctx), fmt_int(a_gen)
    b_ctx_str, b_gen_str = fmt_int(b_ctx), fmt_int(b_gen)
    c_env_str, c_verify_str = fmt_usd(c_env, precision=2), fmt_usd(c_verify, precision=2)
    c_human_str = fmt_usd(c_human, precision=0)
    a_model_str, b_model_str = fmt_usd(a_model, precision=3), fmt_usd(b_model, precision=3)
    a_attempt_str, b_attempt_str = fmt_usd(a_attempt, precision=5), fmt_usd(b_attempt, precision=5)
    a_total_str, b_total_str = fmt_usd(a_total, precision=0), fmt_usd(b_total, precision=3)
    a_total_h_str, b_total_h_str = fmt_usd(a_total_h, precision=0), fmt_usd(b_total_h, precision=3)
    a_eff_str, b_eff_str = fmt_usd(a_eff, precision=2), fmt_usd(b_eff, precision=2)
    a_eff_h_str, b_eff_h_str = fmt_usd(a_eff_h, precision=2), fmt_usd(b_eff_h, precision=2)
    eff_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(eff_ratio, precision=1)
    eff_h_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(eff_h_ratio, precision=1)
```

::: {#nbk-18-the-token-price-fallacy-in-automated .callout-notebook title="The token-price fallacy in automated bug repair"}

**Problem:** Two hypothetical configurations each process the same `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.tickets_str` tickets, with one bounded attempt per ticket and the same acceptance contract. The scenario assumes the fixed per-attempt usage below, including rejected attempts. At the cutoff, all attempts, assessment, and charges are settled; no outcome is pending. The environment charge includes tool use, sandbox holding, and cleanup, while the assessment charge includes the remaining allocated runtime overhead. No additional capacity charge lies outside this example's boundary. Which configuration costs less per accepted repair?

| Parameter                               | Frontier configuration                                                          | Low-token-price configuration                                                   |
|:----------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Input / output price per million tokens | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_in_str` / `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_out_str`  | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_in_str` / `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_out_str`  |
| Turns per attempt                       | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_turns_str`                                        | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_turns_str`                                        |
| Input / output tokens per turn          | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_ctx_str` / `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_gen_str` | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_ctx_str` / `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_gen_str` |
| Accepted tickets                        | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_accepted_str`                                     | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_accepted_str`                                     |
| Environment cost per turn               | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.c_env_str`                                          | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.c_env_str`                                          |
| Additional assessment per attempt       | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.c_verify_str`                                       | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.c_verify_str`                                       |

: **Illustrative Bug-Repair Cohort**: Assumed prices, usage, and accepted counts for two configurations; these are arithmetic inputs, not observed measurements. {#tbl-vol3-token-price-fallacy}

**Math:** Applying the rates and usage in @tbl-vol3-token-price-fallacy gives model charges per attempt of `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_model_str` and `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_model_str`. Adding the other charges gives `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_attempt_str` and `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_attempt_str`, respectively. The complete cohorts therefore cost `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_total_str` and `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_total_str`. Dividing each total by its accepted count gives `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_eff_str` and `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_eff_str` per accepted repair. The lower-token-price configuration costs less per attempt but `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.eff_ratio_mult_str` as much per accepted task.

Now expand both accounting boundaries to include `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.c_human_str` of engineer triage for each rejected attempt. The frontier configuration has `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_rejected_str` rejected tickets and the other has `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_rejected_str`. Total costs become `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_total_h_str` and `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_total_h_str`; costs per accepted task become `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_eff_h_str` and `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_eff_h_str`, a ratio of `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.eff_h_ratio_mult_str`. Triage adds no accepted repairs in this scenario. If engineers also completed tickets, their assessed outcomes and completion costs would require a separate, explicitly named combined service account.

**Systems insight:** The ranking follows from the assumed trajectory costs and acceptance counts, not from model size or a universal acceptance threshold. The calculation does not establish why the configurations differ or predict a new workload. It shows which evidence a real comparison must collect.

:::

Reporting follows from the same account. Acceptance counts and uncertainty, total cost, cost per accepted task, and latency belong to the same cohort and cutoff. Unknown outcomes and unsettled liabilities remain visible. Comparable available resources and budget ceilings do not require identical realized spending. A policy can legitimately spend more to meet a deadline or cover more tasks, provided the objective and constraints precede the comparison. For a positive completed account, accepted tasks per dollar is the reciprocal of $C_{\text{eff}}$; it is useful when that is the chosen objective, not a substitute for acceptance scope or authority limits.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}

↩ Acceptance evidence, matched comparisons, and incomplete outcomes are established in @sec-vol3-evaluation.

:::

The account also identifies the next purchase to examine. In a long trajectory, repeated input can make a substantial contribution to model charges. Prefix reuse and compaction change what the runtime pays to carry that context, while reasoning and retry policies change how many calls it buys.

## Caching and Reasoning Budgets {#sec-vol3-agent-economics-caching}

An input token can appear in many calls without requiring its attention state to be recomputed each time. Conversely, reusing that state need not make the token free. Context engineering and KV-cache management established when reuse is valid; this section prices it. It then asks whether changing the context or purchasing additional attempts lowers cost under the same task-acceptance contract.

### Economic valuation of prefix cache hits

Separate the logical input from the work performed and the amount billed. A service may retain compatible KV state between calls even when the client supplies the full logical transcript again. Let $L_t$ be the logical input length on call $t$, $H_t$ its eligible cached prefix, and $O_t$ its billed output length. For a declared tariff with per-token prices $p_{\mathrm{in}}$, $p_{\mathrm{cache}}$, and $p_{\mathrm{out}}$, the token charge is

$$
C_{\mathrm{session}}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left[p_{\mathrm{in}}(L_t-H_t)+p_{\mathrm{cache}}H_t+p_{\mathrm{out}}O_t\right].
$$

This tariff is a model of billing, not a universal provider contract. Cache-write charges, retention charges, minimum eligible lengths, and other billed categories must be added when applicable. A bill discount also need not reduce usage against a service's request or token quota.

For an append-only transcript whose first prompt has $L_0$ tokens,

$$
L_t=L_0+\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\left(L_{\mathrm{gen},i}+L_{\mathrm{obs},i}\right).
$$

Under the simplifying assumption that each turn appends exactly $\Delta L$ tokens, total logical input is

$$
S_T=T L_0+\Delta L\frac{T(T-1)}{2}.
$$

Under ideal prefix reuse, the first prompt and each appended increment are charged as fresh input once: $F_T=L_0+(T-1)\Delta L$. The input charge is therefore $p_{\mathrm{in}}F_T+p_{\mathrm{cache}}(S_T-F_T)$. For positive $p_{\mathrm{cache}}$ and $\Delta L$, the quadratic term remains; caching lowers its coefficient rather than removing it. These equations count logical and billed input, not GPU memory or prefill operations.

The cache must match the delivered token prefix and the relevant model, configuration, and isolation conditions (principle \ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}). A change early in the prefix can invalidate reuse beyond that point, while a stable prefix before the change may remain reusable. Routing, eviction, and long waits can also change the realized hit rate. Price observed eligible hits under the actual service contract rather than assuming that a stable-looking prompt always receives a discount.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-agent-economics-prefix-cache
#| echo: false
#| output: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PRICE REUSED INPUT AND COMPACTION (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-18-prefix-cache-dollars and @nbk-vol3-compaction-crossing.
# │ Goal: Price logical input and find the first paying compaction horizon.
# │ Show: Cache bill, summary/rebuild cost, and adjacent integer horizons.
# │ How: Declared ideal-reuse tariff; compaction causes a complete cache miss.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from math import ceil
from mlsysim import USD
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_usd, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent

class PrefixCacheCost:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Hypothetical tariff and fixed trajectory) ────────────────
    turns, s0, delta, k_turn = 30, 8_000, 1_500, 200
    p_in, p_out = 3 * USD, 15 * USD  # per million tokens
    cached_share = 0.10
    compact_turn, compact_to, summary_out = 16, 12_000, 1_500

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Bills and incremental compaction cost) ────────────────
    sent = turns * s0 + delta * turns * (turns - 1) // 2
    fresh = s0 + delta * (turns - 1)
    in_nocache = sent * p_in / 1_000_000
    in_cache = (fresh + cached_share * (sent - fresh)) * p_in / 1_000_000
    out_cost = turns * k_turn * p_out / 1_000_000
    total_nocache, total_cache = in_nocache + out_cost, in_cache + out_cost
    cache_ratio = (total_nocache / total_cache).magnitude
    ctx_at = s0 + (compact_turn - 1) * delta
    rest = turns - compact_turn + 1
    first_keep = (delta + (ctx_at - delta) * cached_share) * p_in / 1_000_000
    first_comp = compact_to * p_in / 1_000_000
    summary_cost = first_keep + summary_out * p_out / 1_000_000
    upfront = summary_cost + first_comp - first_keep
    per_turn_saving = (ctx_at - compact_to) * cached_share * p_in / 1_000_000
    breakeven_turns = 1 + ceil((upfront / per_turn_saving).magnitude)
    keep_sum = rest * ctx_at + delta * rest * (rest - 1) // 2
    keep_cost = (rest * delta + cached_share * (keep_sum - rest * delta)) * p_in / 1_000_000
    comp_sum = rest * compact_to + delta * rest * (rest - 1) // 2
    comp_fresh = compact_to + (rest - 1) * delta
    comp_cost = (comp_fresh + cached_share * (comp_sum - comp_fresh)) * p_in / 1_000_000
    comp_total = comp_cost + summary_cost
    gap_before = upfront - (breakeven_turns - 2) * per_turn_saving
    saving_at = (breakeven_turns - 1) * per_turn_saving - upfront

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Independent direct sums and integer crossing) ───────────
    direct_keep, direct_comp = 0 * USD, first_comp
    for j in range(rest):
        direct_keep += (delta + cached_share * (ctx_at + j * delta - delta)) * p_in / 1_000_000
        if j > 0:
            direct_comp += (delta + cached_share * (compact_to + (j - 1) * delta)) * p_in / 1_000_000
    check(abs((direct_keep - keep_cost).to(USD).magnitude) < 1e-12, "Keep sum")
    check(abs((direct_comp - comp_cost).to(USD).magnitude) < 1e-12, "Compact sum")
    check(
        abs(((comp_total - keep_cost) - (upfront - (rest - 1) * per_turn_saving)).to(USD).magnitude) < 1e-12,
        "First-turn incremental cost plus later savings",
    )
    check(gap_before > 0 * USD and saving_at >= 0 * USD, "First integer crossing")
    check(breakeven_turns == 12 and comp_total < keep_cost, "Scenario crossing")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    turns_str, s0_str, delta_str = fmt_int(turns), fmt_int(s0), fmt_int(delta)
    k_turn_str = fmt_int(k_turn)
    p_in_str, p_out_str = fmt_usd(p_in, precision=0), fmt_usd(p_out, precision=0)
    cached_pct_str = fmt_percent(cached_share, precision=0)
    sent_str, fresh_str = fmt_int(sent), fmt_int(fresh)
    in_nocache_str, in_cache_str = fmt_usd(in_nocache, precision=3), fmt_usd(in_cache, precision=3)
    out_cost_str = fmt_usd(out_cost, precision=3)
    total_nocache_str, total_cache_str = fmt_usd(total_nocache, precision=3), fmt_usd(total_cache, precision=3)
    cache_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(cache_ratio, precision=1)
    compact_turn_str, ctx_at_str = fmt_int(compact_turn), fmt_int(ctx_at)
    compact_to_str, summary_out_str = fmt_int(compact_to), fmt_int(summary_out)
    rest_str = fmt_int(rest)
    keep_cost_str, comp_cost_str = fmt_usd(keep_cost, precision=5), fmt_usd(comp_cost, precision=5)
    summary_cost_str, comp_total_str = fmt_usd(summary_cost, precision=5), fmt_usd(comp_total, precision=5)
    upfront_str, per_turn_saving_str = fmt_usd(upfront, precision=5), fmt_usd(per_turn_saving, precision=5)
    breakeven_turns_str, before_str = fmt_int(breakeven_turns), fmt_int(breakeven_turns - 1)
    gap_before_str, saving_at_str = fmt_usd(gap_before, precision=5), fmt_usd(saving_at, precision=5)
```

::: {#nbk-18-prefix-cache-dollars .callout-notebook title="Pricing an append-only trajectory"}

**Problem**: A hypothetical trajectory runs `{python} PrefixCacheCost.turns_str` turns, beginning with `{python} PrefixCacheCost.s0_str` input tokens and appending `{python} PrefixCacheCost.delta_str` tokens per turn. Each call generates `{python} PrefixCacheCost.k_turn_str` output tokens. The tariff charges `{python} PrefixCacheCost.p_in_str` per million fresh input tokens, `{python} PrefixCacheCost.p_out_str` per million output tokens, and `{python} PrefixCacheCost.cached_pct_str` percent of the fresh-input rate for cached reads, with no separate write or retention fee. How much does ideal prefix reuse reduce this trajectory's token bill?

**Math**: Total logical input is `{python} PrefixCacheCost.sent_str` tokens. With ideal reuse, `{python} PrefixCacheCost.fresh_str` are charged at the fresh-input rate. Input therefore costs `{python} PrefixCacheCost.in_nocache_str` without reuse and `{python} PrefixCacheCost.in_cache_str` with it. Adding the unchanged `{python} PrefixCacheCost.out_cost_str` output charge gives `{python} PrefixCacheCost.total_nocache_str` and `{python} PrefixCacheCost.total_cache_str`, a `{python} PrefixCacheCost.cache_ratio_mult_str` ratio.

**Systems insight**: The calculation holds the delivered inputs and generated lengths fixed. It prices reuse, not a capability improvement, and excludes the common tool, assessment, and other trajectory costs. Realized cache misses or additional tariff categories change the bill.

:::

### The price of compaction

Compaction changes the input itself. Replacing old turns with a summary can preserve a stable system prefix, so a complete cache miss is not inevitable. To expose the economic trade-off, consider a declared complete-miss case: the first compacted call has no reusable prefix, while subsequent calls again reuse their append-only history. Compare it with keeping the original cached context over the same remaining calls. Hold future increments and ordinary output costs equal; this is a conditional price comparison, not a claim that summarization preserves behavior.

Let $L$ be the input length at the decision, $M<L$ the compacted length, and $R\ge1$ the remaining ordinary calls, **including the first compacted call**. Suppose the unmodified call adds $\Delta L$ fresh tokens to a cached history. Its input charge is $K_1=p_{\mathrm{in}}\Delta L+p_{\mathrm{cache}}(L-\Delta L)$. If the summary call can reuse that same history and emits $O_s$ tokens, its charge under this scenario is

$$
C_s=K_1+p_{\mathrm{out}}O_s.
$$

A different summarizer or prefix layout requires its actual charge instead. The first compacted ordinary call costs $p_{\mathrm{in}}M$. Relative to not compacting, the upfront increment is therefore $U=C_s+p_{\mathrm{in}}M-K_1$, including both summarization and incremental cache rebuilding. Each later call saves $s=p_{\mathrm{cache}}(L-M)$ under the equal-growth assumption. Thus

$$
C_{\mathrm{compact}}(R)-C_{\mathrm{keep}}(R)=U-(R-1)s,
\qquad
R_{\min}=1+\left\lceil\frac{U}{s}\right\rceil
\quad(U>0,\ s>0).
$$

$R_{\min}$ is the first integer horizon at which compaction costs no more; equality at the crossing is possible. If $U\le0$, the first call already pays back under this model. If $s=0$ and $U>0$, later cached-input savings cannot repay the upfront increment. The distinction between the first call and later calls prevents an off-by-one error in the remaining horizon.

::: {#nbk-vol3-compaction-crossing .callout-notebook title="Count the first compacted call"}

**Problem**: In the preceding scenario, compact at turn `{python} PrefixCacheCost.compact_turn_str`, reducing `{python} PrefixCacheCost.ctx_at_str` tokens to `{python} PrefixCacheCost.compact_to_str`. The summary call emits `{python} PrefixCacheCost.summary_out_str` tokens and receives the stated cached-history pricing. There are `{python} PrefixCacheCost.rest_str` ordinary calls left, including the first compacted one. What is the minimum remaining horizon at which compaction costs no more than keeping the context?

**Math**: Keeping the context costs `{python} PrefixCacheCost.keep_cost_str` in remaining input. Compaction costs `{python} PrefixCacheCost.comp_cost_str` in ordinary input plus `{python} PrefixCacheCost.summary_cost_str` for the summary, or `{python} PrefixCacheCost.comp_total_str`. The upfront increment is `{python} PrefixCacheCost.upfront_str`; each later call saves `{python} PrefixCacheCost.per_turn_saving_str`. With `{python} PrefixCacheCost.before_str` calls left, compaction still costs `{python} PrefixCacheCost.gap_before_str` more. With `{python} PrefixCacheCost.breakeven_turns_str` left, it saves `{python} PrefixCacheCost.saving_at_str`.

**Systems insight**: Payback depends on the remaining horizon and the cache state changed by compaction. The calculation does not establish that the shorter context preserves acceptance. Lost constraints, extra retrieval, or changed trajectory lengths can erase a token saving; better context relevance or fitting the model's input limit can justify compaction even without immediate bill savings.

:::

### Reasoning and retry budgets

The runtime can also purchase more deliberation within a call or more assessed attempts. A configured reasoning limit is a ceiling, not evidence that every call uses it or that more usage improves acceptance. Compare realized billed usage and task outcomes under the same assessment contract. Additional serial generation can increase latency, but a price calculation alone cannot rank end-to-end durations.

For a deliberately simple retry model, assume every task in the comparison has the same per-attempt acceptance probability $p>0$. Conditional on that task's fixed input and environment, attempts are independent draws from the same configuration, each costing $c$ including assessment and other counted work. Sequential retry stops at the first accepted result or after $k$ attempts. Its acceptance probability is $q_k=1-(1-p)^k$, and its expected attempt count is $\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(1-p)^j=q_k/p$. Consequently, expected spend divided by expected accepted tasks is $(cq_k/p)/q_k=c/p$. This is a population ratio under the stated model, not a promise to complete each task or an exact ratio in a small observed cohort.

Launching all $k$ attempts and paying for all of them instead costs $kc/q_k$ per expected accepted task, provided the same assessment can identify and return an accepted candidate. These are bounded policies with different realized spending, not a comparison requiring equal bills. Both must fit the same available resource ceilings and preserve authority and effect-settlement rules.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-agent-economics-retry-budget
#| echo: false
#| output: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PRICE BOUNDED ATTEMPT POLICIES (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-vol3-economics-retry-policies.
# │ Goal: Separate coverage, per-input spend, and cost per accepted task.
# │ Show: Sequential early stop, fully paid batch, and one stronger attempt.
# │ How: Homogeneous conditional iid acceptance and fixed all-in attempt cost.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import USD
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_usd, fmt_percent

class RetryBudget:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Independent hypothetical policy comparison) ──────────────
    p_small, p_big, k = 0.30, 0.70, 5
    c_small, c_big = 0.10 * USD, 0.40 * USD

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Expected costs include rejected attempts) ─────────────
    coverage = 1 - (1 - p_small) ** k
    seq_attempts = 0.0
    for j in range(k):
        seq_attempts += (1 - p_small) ** j
    seq_cost, par_cost = c_small * seq_attempts, k * c_small
    seq_per_acc, par_per_acc = seq_cost / coverage, par_cost / coverage
    big_per_acc = c_big / p_big

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Geometric identity and scenario ordering) ───────────────
    check(abs(seq_attempts - coverage / p_small) < 1e-12, "Expected attempts")
    check(abs((seq_per_acc - c_small / p_small).to(USD).magnitude) < 1e-12, "Cost ratio")
    check(coverage > p_big and seq_per_acc < big_per_acc < par_per_acc, "Scenario comparison")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    p_small_str, p_big_str = fmt(p_small, precision=2), fmt(p_big, precision=2)
    c_small_str, c_big_str = fmt_usd(c_small, precision=2), fmt_usd(c_big, precision=2)
    k_str, coverage_str = fmt_int(k), fmt_percent(coverage, precision=1)
    seq_attempts_str = fmt(seq_attempts, precision=3)
    seq_cost_str, par_cost_str = fmt_usd(seq_cost, precision=3), fmt_usd(par_cost, precision=3)
    seq_per_acc_str = fmt_usd(seq_per_acc, precision=3)
    par_per_acc_str, big_per_acc_str = fmt_usd(par_per_acc, precision=3), fmt_usd(big_per_acc, precision=3)
```

::: {#nbk-vol3-economics-retry-policies .callout-notebook title="What a retry cap buys"}

**Problem**: A cheap configuration has acceptance probability `{python} RetryBudget.p_small_str` and all-in cost `{python} RetryBudget.c_small_str` per attempt. A stronger configuration has probability `{python} RetryBudget.p_big_str` and costs `{python} RetryBudget.c_big_str`. Allow up to `{python} RetryBudget.k_str` cheap attempts under the model above. Which policy has the lowest cost per expected accepted task: sequential retry, a fully paid batch, or one stronger attempt?

**Math**: Sequential retry accepts `{python} RetryBudget.coverage_str` percent of inputs in expectation and uses `{python} RetryBudget.seq_attempts_str` attempts per input. Expected spend is `{python} RetryBudget.seq_cost_str` per input and `{python} RetryBudget.seq_per_acc_str` per accepted task. Paying for the full batch gives the same acceptance probability for `{python} RetryBudget.par_cost_str` per input and `{python} RetryBudget.par_per_acc_str` per accepted task. One stronger attempt costs `{python} RetryBudget.big_per_acc_str` per accepted task.

**Systems insight**: Sequential retry is cheaper per accepted task and has higher acceptance than the single stronger attempt in this stipulated example. No durations or queueing data were supplied, so the calculation does not identify the fastest policy. A fully paid batch may trade extra work for a deadline benefit; that benefit must be measured.

:::

Real tasks need not share one $p$. Even with independent sampling conditional on each task, hard tasks can retain low acceptance across retries. Averaging task-specific probabilities before applying $1-(1-p)^k$ generally gives the wrong coverage, and the aggregate cost ratio need not remain $c/p$. Feedback, changing inputs, outages, and shared mutable environments can also invalidate the fixed-attempt model. Identical weights alone do not prove dependent draws. Use the measured task-level retry outcomes and costs established by the evaluation protocol.

The acceptance procedure also retains its limitations. Additional candidates can create additional opportunities for false acceptance; a passing check is evidence under its declared scope, not an authorization to publish or a guarantee of correctness. Bounded retries limit purchased work while unresolved effects and charges retain owners. Caching, compaction, and retry policy therefore change the bill under explicit assumptions. The next section asks which purchased work actually determines the completion time.

## Critical-Path Latency {#sec-vol3-agent-economics-criticalpath}

A faster model call does not produce an equally faster repair. Tests, environment preparation, queueing, and finalization can occupy most of the elapsed interval. The economic question is how much a proposed change reduces time to a declared endpoint, what resources it consumes, and whether it preserves the required acceptance evidence. A trace helps locate that opportunity; it does not by itself establish the value of buying it.

### Account for dependencies and elapsed time

The tracing discipline in @sec-vol3-evaluation-tracing distinguishes an enclosing span from the work inside it. Adding a parent duration to its children's durations double-counts time. Adding concurrent children also overcounts elapsed time, while omitting queueing or uninstrumented gaps undercounts it. Preserve unexplained intervals as unexplained rather than assigning them to a convenient component.

A span's parent identifies containment, not necessarily a completion dependency. Construct the execution graph from the actual dispatch and join conditions: an edge means that the later interval cannot begin before its predecessor finishes. Use nonoverlapping intervals along each path, not inclusive parents alongside their children. For a dependency graph with durations $t(v)$ and source-to-sink paths $\Pi$, its longest path is

$$T_{\text{critical}} = \max_{\pi \in \Pi} \sum_{v \in \pi} t(v).$$ {#eq-vol3-critical-path}

For a graph containing only required service work, @eq-vol3-critical-path is a lower bound on completion time. It represents the observed elapsed interval exactly only when the graph also accounts for actual release times, resource waits, and other delays at the chosen boundary. The observation boundary must include whatever the decision values: a streamed answer, an assessed candidate, and a fully finalized task are different endpoints.

Shortening a nonlimiting branch need not shorten that endpoint under a fixed schedule, but it can release capacity or lower cost. Shortening the current longest path can make another path limiting. Recompute the paths after the proposed change rather than subtracting every saved component-second from the trajectory's elapsed time.

### Bound the payoff of faster inference

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-agent-economics-critical-path
#| echo: false
# WHERE FASTER INFERENCE HELPS (LEGO)
# Goal: Bound elapsed-time savings in one fixed, serial repair episode.
# Scope: Hypothetical seconds, not measurements or a fleet workload model.
from mlsysim import second
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_qty, fmt_percent, fmt_multiple, check

class CriticalPath:
    # 1. LOAD: sequential intervals; all required work remains unchanged.
    model_intervals_s = (1.20, 8.40, 1.85, 11.20, 2.10, 4.50)
    tests_s = 245.60
    lifecycle_intervals_s = (14.80, 22.55)
    runtime_status_intervals_s = (0.12, 0.08)
    model_speedup = 4.0

    # 2. EXECUTE: each interval belongs to exactly one category.
    model_s = sum(model_intervals_s)
    lifecycle_s = sum(lifecycle_intervals_s)
    runtime_status_s = sum(runtime_status_intervals_s)
    other_s = tests_s + lifecycle_s + runtime_status_s
    total_s = model_s + other_s
    model_fraction = model_s / total_s
    changed_s = other_s + model_s / model_speedup
    saving_s = total_s - changed_s
    speedup = total_s / changed_s
    limiting_speedup = total_s / other_s

    # 3. GUARD: disjoint accounting and independent Amdahl calculation.
    check(all(t >= 0 for t in model_intervals_s + lifecycle_intervals_s + runtime_status_intervals_s), "Nonnegative intervals")
    check(tests_s >= 0 and other_s > 0 and model_speedup >= 1, "Valid acceleration domain")
    check(abs(total_s - 312.40) < 1e-9, "Full declared elapsed interval")
    check(abs(changed_s - total_s * (1 - model_fraction + model_fraction / model_speedup)) < 1e-9, "Independent Amdahl calculation")
    check(abs(saving_s - 21.9375) < 1e-9, "Independent saved model time")
    check(1 <= speedup <= limiting_speedup, "Finite acceleration respects limiting bound")

    # 4. OUTPUT: each export is used below, with units supplied once.
    model_str = fmt_qty(model_s * second, second, precision=2)
    tests_str = fmt_qty(tests_s * second, second, precision=2)
    lifecycle_str = fmt_qty(lifecycle_s * second, second, precision=2)
    runtime_status_str = fmt_qty(runtime_status_s * second, second, precision=2)
    total_str = fmt_qty(total_s * second, second, precision=2)
    fraction_str = fmt_percent(model_fraction, precision=1, style="prose")
    model_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(model_speedup, precision=0)
    changed_str = fmt_qty(changed_s * second, second, precision=2)
    saving_str = fmt_qty(saving_s * second, second, precision=2)
    speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(speedup, precision=2)
    limiting_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(limiting_speedup, precision=2)
```

::: {#nbk-18-critical-path-investment .callout-notebook title="How much does faster inference buy?"}

**Problem**: Estimate the elapsed-time benefit of faster model calls in a hypothetical three-turn repair episode.

**Assumptions**: All intervals execute sequentially, from runtime initialization through required sandbox snapshot export. The grouped durations in @tbl-vol3-trace-critical-path are disjoint sums, not nested spans or a chronological listing. The test duration includes the scenario's required checks. No additional queueing, overlap, or unaccounted interval exists. The hypothetical intervention accelerates all model intervals without changing outputs, tool work, evidence coverage, scheduling, or finalization. This is a timing scenario, not a measured acceptance rate or cost estimate.

| Disjoint category                            |                               Elapsed time |
|:---------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------:|
| Model calls across the three turns           |          `{python} CriticalPath.model_str` |
| Required test execution                      |          `{python} CriticalPath.tests_str` |
| Sandbox creation and snapshot export         |      `{python} CriticalPath.lifecycle_str` |
| Runtime initialization and repository status | `{python} CriticalPath.runtime_status_str` |
| **Whole declared interval**                  |      **`{python} CriticalPath.total_str`** |

: **One serial repair episode**: Categories partition elapsed time under the stated assumptions; the total is not an additional interval. {#tbl-vol3-trace-critical-path}

**Calculation**: If model work occupies fraction $f$ of the original time $T$ and becomes $s$ times faster, with $s \geq 1$, then $T' = T[(1-f)+f/s]$. Here model work occupies `{python} CriticalPath.fraction_str`. A `{python} CriticalPath.model_speedup_mult_str` model acceleration gives a projected `{python} CriticalPath.changed_str` episode, saving `{python} CriticalPath.saving_str` and yielding a whole-episode speedup of `{python} CriticalPath.speedup_mult_str`. Even instantaneous model work would give only `{python} CriticalPath.limiting_speedup_mult_str` under these assumptions.

**Systems insight**: The bound limits this intervention's elapsed-time benefit, not its monetary value. A small saving may matter near a deadline, and a model optimization may also lower resource use. Conversely, a faster serving tier may cost more. Compare that trade-off with changes to the longer test and lifecycle intervals, preserving the same acceptance contract. In a branching trajectory, recompute @eq-vol3-critical-path; this serial fraction calculation does not establish the bound for a changed schedule.

:::

### Shorten the path without weakening the result

Independent tool calls can overlap when their dependencies, authority, and resource reservations permit it. If they start together, do not interfere, and all must finish before continuation, the join waits for the longest call rather than their sum. Shared resource contention, staggered starts, or one call consuming another's output invalidate that simple comparison. Cached builds and warm environments likewise require valid reuse and the isolation and reset conditions already established for execution and evaluation.

Preparation can sometimes overlap model generation, but a partially streamed call is not an authorized request. Any speculative preparation needs its own current scope and resource admission. It must not perform the proposed external effect before complete validation and authorization. Even a file read can cross an access boundary or expose data; calling preparation read-only does not make it safe. Count discarded preparation and release its resources when the completed proposal does not use it.

Early stopping changes the observation as well as its duration. A failed mandatory test can establish that a candidate fails that criterion without running every remaining check. It does not establish which other checks would fail, and stopping after an early pass does not establish that the whole suite passes. Test selection and streaming failures can accelerate diagnosis, but final acceptance still needs its declared coverage. Cancellation also leaves accounting obligations until outstanding work has settled, as the recovery chapters established.

### Profitability boundaries for speculative decoding {#sec-vol3-agent-economics-speculative}

@Sec-vol3-foundation-model introduced speculative decoding as a serving technique whose output and performance depend on its implementation and sampling assumptions. Here its role is an economic option: does it improve the task-level objective enough to justify its resource cost?

Evaluate the complete serving path, including draft generation, target verification, coordination, setup, and work discarded at rejection or early stopping. Short responses and interrupted calls can spend resources on proposals whose tokens never become usable output. Acceptance by a draft verifier is not acceptance of the repair task. A draft-token acceptance rate alone therefore establishes neither elapsed-time savings nor cost per accepted task, and output labels such as code or planning do not supply a universal ranking.

Measure the candidate policy under the intended load and memory constraints. A draft model occupies resources that might otherwise serve another request; verification changes the target's work and scheduling. Those opportunity costs matter even when one call becomes faster. Neither idle arithmetic nor a long queue alone decides the policy. Compare complete-call latency, total resource use or billable charges, queueing effects, and downstream task acceptance against the same baseline workload and available ceilings.

Then place the measured call-level change back into the trajectory. An acceleration on a limiting path may buy deadline headroom; one elsewhere may primarily buy capacity or cost savings. A policy can be worth purchasing despite higher expense when the time benefit is valuable, or worth rejecting despite faster token generation when contention erases that benefit. The decision is conditional on the workload and objective, not a universal model-share threshold.

::: {#chk-18-whole-trajectory-economics .callout-checkpoint title="Cost and time per accepted task"}

Before routing calls across models, check the accounting so far:

- [ ] **Failed attempts**: Which costs remain in the numerator when an initiated attempt fails, is canceled, or still awaits settlement?
- [ ] **Cache layout**: Which prefix and service-validity conditions must hold before a reused logical input receives a reuse benefit?
- [ ] **Compaction**: Why can summary generation and cache rebuilding outweigh savings over a short remaining horizon?
- [ ] **Critical path**: What assumptions make the serial speedup calculation valid, and why must a branching trajectory be recalculated after an intervention?

:::

Timing analysis asks where acceleration changes the task's outcome or resource demand. Routing asks a complementary question: which model or sequence of models can satisfy the same acceptance contract at an acceptable cost and latency?

## Model Cascades and Routing {#sec-vol3-agent-economics-cascades}

Critical-path analysis identifies where faster execution matters. Routing asks a complementary question: which configuration should attempt the work at all? A specialized model may complete a constrained transformation inexpensively, while another configuration may be worth its higher cost for diagnosis. A *model cascade* tries one configuration and conditionally escalates to another, an approach explored in FrugalGPT [@chen2023frugalgpt]. Its economic value depends on what the lower tiers resolve, what their failures cost, and which tasks remain for later tiers.

Every exit must satisfy the same declared task or subtask acceptance contract. A schema check can suffice when the assigned task is purely a syntactic transformation; it cannot establish that a source patch preserves authentication behavior. Calling a more capable model does not strengthen the contract automatically, and choosing a cheaper model does not justify weakening it. Acceptance checks supply scoped evidence, not a guarantee that the accepted candidate has no latent defects. Publication and effect authorization remain separate runtime decisions.

### Direct routing and conditional escalation

A direct router selects a configuration before generation, using available task features. A cascade instead buys an initial attempt and uses its assessment to decide whether to continue. These policies need different accounts. A mistaken direct route can reduce acceptance or miss a deadline. A mistaken cheap-first choice can consume budget and time before escalation, even when the later tier eventually resolves the task. Neither error is made harmless by placing a check afterward.

For a three-tier cascade, let $q_j$ be the probability of acceptance at tier $j$, conditional on reaching it. Assume every task not accepted at a lower tier continues to the next tier, with no additional retry, cancellation, or stopping branch. The reach probabilities are $r_1=1$, $r_2=1-q_1$, and $r_3=(1-q_1)(1-q_2)$. The product is the probability chain rule, not an assumption that tiers fail independently. Later tiers receive the selected remainder, so their conditional acceptance rates cannot be copied from a full-workload benchmark.

Let $c_j$ be mean generation and associated execution cost conditional on reaching tier $j$, excluding its gate, and let $g_j$ be that gate's mean cost. Let $t_j$ and $v_j$ be the corresponding mean durations. Count preparation, assessment, and cleanup in the appropriate terms rather than pricing only output tokens. Linearity of expectation gives

$$
\mathbb{E}[C_{\mathrm{cascade}}]=\sum_{j=1}^{3}r_j(c_j+g_j),
\qquad p_{\mathrm{acc}}=\sum_{j=1}^{3}r_jq_j.
$$

For a serial cascade with all elapsed intervals represented, its mean duration is

$$
\mathbb{E}[T_{\mathrm{cascade}}]=\sum_{j=1}^{3}r_j(t_j+v_j).
$$

The final tier pays for its gate too. With fixed durations, a task reaching every tier takes $\sum_j(t_j+v_j)$; with variable durations and queueing, that fixed sum is not a worst-case bound or a tail percentile. If the policy permits earlier stopping or unresolved assessments, use its actual reach probabilities and retain those outcomes separately.

The economic comparison returns to the chapter's denominator. For completed cohorts, divide total incurred cost by the observed number accepted under the declared contract. The planning analogue is $\mathbb{E}[C_{\mathrm{cascade}}]/p_{\mathrm{acc}}$ when $p_{\mathrm{acc}}>0$, not the cost of just the successful paths. It is a ratio of population quantities, not the expected value of every finite sample's ratio. A direct frontier policy needs its own acceptance rate on the full target cohort; its rate on the harder escalated subset is not that baseline.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-agent-economics-cascade
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ COST AND ACCEPTANCE OF A THREE-TIER CASCADE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The routing comparison under one unchanged acceptance contract.
# │ Goal: Price every reached tier, including its final assessment.
# │ Show: Resolved counts, cost per accepted task, and fixed-scenario durations.
# │ How: Reconcile a hypothetical completed cohort with conditional reach sums.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import ureg
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_percent, fmt_time, fmt_usd

class CascadeCost:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    tasks = 100_000  # hypothetical completed cohort per policy
    calls = (0.0004, 0.0020, 0.0600)  # dollars per reached tier, gate excluded
    gate_cost = 0.0010  # dollars per assessment, same contract at every tier
    call_seconds = (0.25, 0.80, 4.50)
    gate_seconds = 0.40
    accepted_by_tier = (60_000, 28_000, 11_400)
    direct_accepted = 97_000  # separate stipulated full-cohort baseline

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    reached = (tasks, tasks - accepted_by_tier[0], tasks - accepted_by_tier[0] - accepted_by_tier[1])
    spend, elapsed_sum = 0.0, 0.0
    conditional, reaches = [], []
    for j in range(3):
        conditional.append(accepted_by_tier[j] / reached[j])
        reaches.append(reached[j] / tasks)
        spend += reached[j] * (calls[j] + gate_cost)
        elapsed_sum += reached[j] * (call_seconds[j] + gate_seconds)
    accepted = sum(accepted_by_tier)
    unresolved = tasks - accepted
    per_initiated = spend / tasks
    per_accepted = spend / accepted
    direct_spend = tasks * (calls[-1] + gate_cost)
    direct_per_accepted = direct_spend / direct_accepted
    mean_seconds = elapsed_sum / tasks
    all_tiers_seconds = sum(call_seconds) + 3 * gate_seconds
    direct_seconds = call_seconds[-1] + gate_seconds

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(tasks > 0 and 0 < direct_accepted <= tasks, "baseline denominator")
    check(all(0 <= q <= 1 for q in conditional), "conditional acceptance")
    check(accepted + unresolved == tasks and accepted > 0, "cohort conservation")
    check(math.isclose(reaches[2], (1 - conditional[0]) * (1 - conditional[1])), "conditional reach chain")
    expected_cost = 0.0
    for r, c in zip(reaches, calls):
        expected_cost += r * (c + gate_cost)
    check(math.isclose(per_initiated, expected_cost), "cost ledger matches expectation")
    check(per_accepted < direct_per_accepted, "stipulated cost comparison")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    tasks_str = fmt_int(tasks)
    call_costs_str = ", ".join(fmt_usd(c, precision=4) for c in calls)
    call_times_str = ", ".join(fmt_time(t, ureg.second, precision=2) for t in call_seconds)
    gate_cost_str = fmt_usd(gate_cost, precision=4)
    gate_time_str = fmt_time(gate_seconds, ureg.second, precision=2)
    first_accepted_str = fmt_int(accepted_by_tier[0])
    second_accepted_str = fmt_int(accepted_by_tier[1])
    third_accepted_str = fmt_int(accepted_by_tier[2])
    second_reached_str = fmt_int(reached[1])
    third_reached_str = fmt_int(reached[2])
    conditional_rates_str = ", ".join(fmt_percent(q, precision=0, style="prose") for q in conditional)
    direct_accepted_str = fmt_int(direct_accepted)
    accepted_str = fmt_int(accepted)
    unresolved_str = fmt_int(unresolved)
    acceptance_str = fmt_percent(accepted / tasks, precision=1, style="prose")
    spend_str = fmt_usd(spend, precision=0)
    per_initiated_str = fmt_usd(per_initiated, precision=5)
    per_accepted_str = fmt_usd(per_accepted, precision=5)
    direct_spend_str = fmt_usd(direct_spend, precision=0)
    direct_per_accepted_str = fmt_usd(direct_per_accepted, precision=5)
    mean_time_str = fmt_time(mean_seconds, ureg.second, precision=3)
    all_tiers_time_str = fmt_time(all_tiers_seconds, ureg.second, precision=2)
    direct_time_str = fmt_time(direct_seconds, ureg.second, precision=2)
```

::: {#nbk-18-cost-and-latency-trade-offs-in .callout-notebook title="Price the accepted result at every exit"}

**Problem:** For hypothetical cohorts of `{python} CascadeCost.tasks_str` small source-editing tasks per policy, should a team choose the cascade or direct frontier execution to minimize cost per accepted result, and what duration trade-off accompanies that choice?

**Assumptions:** Every candidate faces the same scoped acceptance procedure. In tier order, the cascade's generation and execution charges, excluding assessment, are `{python} CascadeCost.call_costs_str` per reached tier, with fixed durations of `{python} CascadeCost.call_times_str`. Each assessment costs `{python} CascadeCost.gate_cost_str` and takes `{python} CascadeCost.gate_time_str`, including the final one. These stipulated charges include all execution, cleanup, and allocated shared overhead within the example's boundary; there is no queue wait or human completion, and all bills and assessments are settled at the cutoff.

The cascade accepts `{python} CascadeCost.first_accepted_str` tasks at tier 1, `{python} CascadeCost.second_accepted_str` of the `{python} CascadeCost.second_reached_str` reaching tier 2, and `{python} CascadeCost.third_accepted_str` of the `{python} CascadeCost.third_reached_str` reaching tier 3. The conditional acceptance rates are therefore `{python} CascadeCost.conditional_rates_str`, respectively. For comparison, a separate direct-to-frontier policy is stipulated to accept `{python} CascadeCost.direct_accepted_str` of its equally sized full cohort. That full-cohort rate is an independent scenario input, not inferred from the cascade's selected remainder. A real comparison would measure both policies on comparable task populations with comparable available resource ceilings.

**Calculation:** The cascade accepts `{python} CascadeCost.accepted_str` tasks, or `{python} CascadeCost.acceptance_str`, and leaves `{python} CascadeCost.unresolved_str` unaccepted. It spends `{python} CascadeCost.spend_str` in total: `{python} CascadeCost.per_initiated_str` per initiated task and `{python} CascadeCost.per_accepted_str` per accepted result. Direct frontier execution spends `{python} CascadeCost.direct_spend_str`, or `{python} CascadeCost.direct_per_accepted_str` per accepted result. The lower-tier attempts are paid for whether or not they pass.

Under the fixed-duration assumptions, the cascade takes `{python} CascadeCost.mean_time_str` on average, while its all-tier path takes `{python} CascadeCost.all_tiers_time_str`. Direct execution takes `{python} CascadeCost.direct_time_str`, including assessment.

**Decision:** Choose the cascade for the stated cost-per-accepted-result objective if its duration profile is acceptable. A deadline that excludes its all-tier path can instead favor direct routing for selected tasks. This decision is conditional on the scenario: the calculation establishes neither real-world tail latency nor statistical confidence in the stipulated acceptance rates.

:::

### Gate errors and the decision to continue

The cost ledger counts gate decisions even when a gate is wrong. An observed accepted result is not automatically a correct result under every intended property. To price an additional consequence, define $F$ as the event that an initiated task is accepted yet violates an independently assessed criterion, and define $H$ as its additional harm or remediation cost not already included in the execution ledger. The expected cost per initiated task including this term is

$$
\mathbb{E}[C_{\mathrm{with\ harm}}]
=\mathbb{E}[C_{\mathrm{cascade}}]+P(F)\mathbb{E}[H\mid F].
$$

This does not redefine cost per accepted task. A measured false-accept fraction among accepted results must be multiplied by the acceptance probability to obtain $P(F)$ over initiated tasks. A false-positive rate measured among invalid candidates uses a different denominator again. Estimate the relevant event population and uncertainty rather than multiplying an unspecified error rate by a recovery price. Some consequences cannot be repaired; monetary expectation does not replace authority constraints or required risk limits.

Escalation should preserve bounded diagnostic evidence and the identity of the failed candidate. It need not copy the entire failed transcript, but deleting the candidate indiscriminately can remove information needed to diagnose its failure. Treat its contents as untrusted, retrieve relevant spans when authorized, and keep pending or unavailable assessments distinct from definite rejection. A passing assessment yields an accepted-candidate record; it does not call an unrestricted commit operation. Publication still checks current dependencies, authority, and any required operation-bound approval.

A learned router can estimate the probability and cost of each eligible remaining policy from evaluation data. Its training records must reflect which configurations were actually tried; logs from a selective router do not reveal every untried configuration's counterfactual result. For a simple monetary objective, suppose policies $A$ and $B$ offer acceptance probabilities $p_A,p_B$ and expected additional costs $C_A,C_B$ conditional on the current task information. If the same accepted outcome is valued at $V$, rejected outcomes have zero value, and other consequences are equal or already counted, prefer $B$ when

$$
V(p_B-p_A)>C_B-C_A.
$$

For direct routing, compare two complete direct policies. After a failed cheap attempt, compare the remaining escalation policy with stopping or another eligible action; already incurred spend is not charged again as an avoidable cost. A cheap-then-frontier policy has its own reach-weighted cost and acceptance probability, not merely the cheap model's price. This expected-value rule applies only within the declared objective and constraints, including remaining budget and deadline. It is not permission to spend past a limit or to substitute economic value for authorization.

Load can change that comparison. Waiting for a tier consumes elapsed time and may retain a sandbox or other resources; another eligible route can become preferable even if its call price is higher. Current queue information therefore belongs in the estimates of remaining cost and completion time. The next section supplies the capacity model needed to reason about those waits without treating a routing choice as a guaranteed latency bound.

## Capacity for Trajectories {#sec-vol3-agent-economics-capacity}

A routing policy changes the work arriving at each model and tool service. Capacity planning asks whether those services can sustain that work within the task's latency and resource constraints. The unit entering the platform is a trajectory; the units entering its bottlenecks are model calls, tool operations, and resource leases. Their arrival rates and residence times are different.

### Residence, service, and quota

For a stable population with finite long-run averages, Little's law relates the mean number of admitted trajectories present, $L_{\text{traj}}$, to their admission rate $\lambda_{\text{traj}}$ and mean time from admission to departure, $\mathbb{E}[T_{\text{traj}}]$ [@little1961]:

$$L_{\text{traj}} = \lambda_{\text{traj}}\mathbb{E}[T_{\text{traj}}].$$ {#eq-vol3-trajectory-concurrency}

The population and boundary must match. Rejected arrivals do not enter this population, while admitted attempts that eventually fail do. A trajectory waiting for approval is still present, but it need not occupy a model worker. Apply the same accounting separately to sandbox leases, retained attention state, active model service, and unsettled operations, using each resource's actual holding intervals. Suspending a trajectory can release one resource while retaining another; neither scheduling state nor local cancellation proves that remote work has settled. @Sec-vol3-appendix-inference-queueing works a tool-wait example that separates live-trajectory counts from attention-state occupancy under different retention policies.

Little's law gives a mean, not a peak concurrency limit or a buffer size that meets a latency percentile. The holding policy and observed occupancy distribution determine how much reserve to provision. Likewise, call demand follows the number of calls per admitted attempt, including retries and delegated calls within the accounting boundary. Under stable flow, its mean rate is $\lambda_{\text{call}}=\lambda_{\text{traj}}\mathbb{E}[N_{\text{call}}]$. This does not make the call arrivals independent: a cohort reaching the same tool boundary can create a burst.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-agent-economics-trajectory-capacity
#| echo: false
from mlsysim import *

class TrajectoryCapacity:
    # 1. LOAD: hypothetical stationary admitted population; token counts
    # include all input/output tokens charged against this scenario's quota.
    arrival = 1 / minute
    residence = 20 * minute
    calls = 60
    tokens_per_call = 30_000
    quota = 2_000_000 / minute

    # 2. EXECUTE: mean resource demand, not burst or deadline feasibility.
    concurrent = (arrival * residence).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    call_rate = arrival * calls
    tokens_per_trajectory = calls * tokens_per_call
    demand = arrival * tokens_per_trajectory
    quota_share = (demand / quota).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    arrival_ceiling = quota / tokens_per_trajectory

    # 3. GUARD
    check(arrival > 0 / minute and residence > 0 * second, "Positive flow and residence")
    check(calls > 0 and tokens_per_call > 0 and quota > 0 / minute, "Positive demand inputs")
    check(0 < quota_share < 1, "This scenario fits the mean token quota only")

    # 4. OUTPUT
    arrival_str = fmt_qty(arrival, 1 / minute, precision=0)
    residence_str = fmt_time(residence, minute, precision=0, style="word")
    calls_str = fmt_int(calls)
    tokens_per_call_str = fmt_int(tokens_per_call)
    quota_str = fmt_qty(quota, 1 / minute, precision=0, commas=True)
    concurrent_str = fmt(concurrent, precision=0)
    call_rate_str = fmt_qty(call_rate, 1 / minute, precision=0)
    tokens_per_trajectory_str = fmt_int(tokens_per_trajectory)
    demand_str = fmt_qty(demand, 1 / minute, precision=0, commas=True)
    quota_share_str = fmt_percent(quota_share, precision=0, style="prose")
    arrival_ceiling_str = fmt_qty(arrival_ceiling, 1 / minute, precision=2)
```

::: {#nbk-18-trajectory-residence-and-quota .callout-notebook title="One arrival rate, different resource demands"}

**Problem**: A hypothetical fleet has a trajectory admission rate of `{python} TrajectoryCapacity.arrival_str`; an attempt remains present for `{python} TrajectoryCapacity.residence_str` on average. It makes `{python} TrajectoryCapacity.calls_str` calls on average, each consuming `{python} TrajectoryCapacity.tokens_per_call_str` quota-accounted tokens on average across calls. In this scenario the provider counts input and output tokens, including cached input, toward a shared token-rate allowance of `{python} TrajectoryCapacity.quota_str`. What mean concurrency and token demand does this imply?

**Model**: Apply @eq-vol3-trajectory-concurrency to admitted attempts, and multiply the long-run call rate by mean tokens per call. The token average is call-weighted; it is not the unweighted mean of per-task averages.

**Result**: Mean trajectory concurrency is `{python} TrajectoryCapacity.concurrent_str`, while the mean call arrival rate is `{python} TrajectoryCapacity.call_rate_str`. The mean token demand is `{python} TrajectoryCapacity.tokens_per_trajectory_str` per trajectory, giving a token rate of `{python} TrajectoryCapacity.demand_str` and using `{python} TrajectoryCapacity.quota_share_str` of the allowance. The quota alone permits a trajectory admission rate of at most `{python} TrajectoryCapacity.arrival_ceiling_str` at this workload mix in the long run.

**Systems insight**: None of these means proves that a burst fits, that a call starts before its deadline, or that the fleet needs one resident sandbox per trajectory. Those conclusions require the quota's actual window and admission semantics, the resource-holding policy, and workload traces.

:::

Provider limits can count requests, tokens, concurrent calls, or other units over different scopes and windows. Admission must obey the actual contract rather than assume a universal pair of token buckets. A billing discount for cached input does not imply quota relief. Reserving capacity for already admitted work can be a useful policy, but the money already spent is not by itself a reason to prioritize that work. Remaining resource needs, deadlines, fairness, and expected task value inform the choice; no reservation based only on mean demand guarantees completion.

### The price of queueing

A small queueing model shows why spare capacity can have economic value. Consider one nonpreemptive, first-come-first-served server with a stationary renewal arrival stream: interarrival times are independent and identically distributed, service times are independent and identically distributed, and the two sequences are independent. Both have finite means and variances. There is no batching, priority, abandonment, or feedback in this model. Let $A$ be an interarrival time, $S$ a service time, and $\lambda_{\text{call}}=1/\mathbb{E}[A]$. Define the squared coefficients of variation $c_a^2=\operatorname{Var}(A)/\mathbb{E}[A]^2$ and $c_s^2=\operatorname{Var}(S)/\mathbb{E}[S]^2$, and utilization $\rho=\lambda_{\text{call}}\mathbb{E}[S]<1$.

For this single-server setting, the Kingman heavy-traffic approximation estimates the mean time waiting *before* service:

$$\mathbb{E}[W_q] \approx \frac{c_a^2+c_s^2}{2}\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}\mathbb{E}[S].$$ {#eq-vol3-kingman-gg1}

The heavy-traffic limit explains the rapid growth near full utilization; the displayed expression is an approximation at a finite load, not an exact mean or a percentile guarantee. A primary derivation and error analysis are given by [Boon, Janssen, and van Leeuwaarden](https://arxiv.org/html/2206.09844). Correlated agent bursts, batched inference, multiple workers, and shared quotas require models or trace-driven simulations that represent those features; replacing the service rate by a pooled rate does not establish a multi-server version of this equation.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-agent-economics-queue-price
#| echo: false
from mlsysim import *

class QueuePrice:
    # 1. LOAD: illustrative single-server model just specified in the text.
    service = 1 * second
    ca2, cs2 = 2.0, 4.0
    rho_low, rho_high = 0.70, 0.90
    holding_dollars_per_second = 0.002

    # 2. EXECUTE
    variability = (ca2 + cs2) / 2
    wait_low = variability * rho_low / (1 - rho_low) * service
    wait_high = variability * rho_high / (1 - rho_high) * service
    holding_low = wait_low.to(second).magnitude * holding_dollars_per_second
    holding_high = wait_high.to(second).magnitude * holding_dollars_per_second

    # 3. GUARD
    check(service > 0 * second and ca2 >= 0 and cs2 >= 0, "Valid mean and variability")
    check(0 < rho_low < rho_high < 1, "Both modeled queues are stable")
    check(holding_dollars_per_second >= 0 and wait_high > wait_low, "Nonnegative holding cost")

    # 4. OUTPUT
    service_str = fmt_time(service, second, precision=0, style="word")
    ca2_str = fmt(ca2, precision=0)
    cs2_str = fmt(cs2, precision=0)
    rho_low_str = fmt_percent(rho_low, precision=0, style="prose")
    rho_high_str = fmt_percent(rho_high, precision=0, style="prose")
    wait_low_str = fmt_time(wait_low, second, precision=0, style="word")
    wait_high_str = fmt_time(wait_high, second, precision=0, style="word")
    holding_rate_str = fmt_usd(holding_dollars_per_second, precision=3)
    holding_low_str = fmt_usd(holding_low, precision=3)
    holding_high_str = fmt_usd(holding_high, precision=3)
```

::: {#nbk-18-sizing-queue-capacity-and-tail .callout-notebook title="Pricing mean queue delay"}

**Problem**: In the hypothetical single-server model above, mean service takes `{python} QueuePrice.service_str`, $c_a^2$ is `{python} QueuePrice.ca2_str`, and $c_s^2$ is `{python} QueuePrice.cs2_str`. A waiting call holds resources costing `{python} QueuePrice.holding_rate_str` per second. How do estimated mean wait and holding cost change between `{python} QueuePrice.rho_low_str` and `{python} QueuePrice.rho_high_str` utilization?

**Model**: Use @eq-vol3-kingman-gg1, then multiply mean wait by the stated linear holding rate. This rate includes only resources retained during the queue interval; it excludes model service, tool execution, and any separate valuation of user delay.

**Result**: Estimated mean wait rises from `{python} QueuePrice.wait_low_str` to `{python} QueuePrice.wait_high_str`, and the corresponding holding charge rises from `{python} QueuePrice.holding_low_str` to `{python} QueuePrice.holding_high_str` per call.

**Systems insight**: Higher occupancy purchases more throughput from the same server while increasing delay and holding cost in this model. Neither utilization is a universal operating target. Validate the estimate and measure the required latency percentiles before choosing reserve capacity.

:::

This is where load enters the routing decision from @sec-vol3-agent-economics-cascades. Compare eligible *remaining paths*, including their queue and service delays, retained-resource costs, verification, and escalation. A nominally cheap tier may lose its advantage when its queue lengthens, but bypassing it is justified only by that full comparison under the same acceptance contract. Changing routing also changes arrival rates, so a delay estimate measured under the old policy need not remain valid. Separate interactive and batch capacity or priority scheduling may help a particular workload; they also change fairness and queue behavior and must be evaluated rather than assumed to improve every trajectory.

### Dedicated capacity versus per-token APIs

Dedicated capacity replaces some usage-proportional charges with a commitment paid while resources are idle as well as busy. Compare the alternatives only after establishing equivalent effective capability, task acceptance criteria, privacy and authority constraints, and feasible latency at the workload mix. Nominally similar model names or token rates do not establish equivalence.

Let $q$ be delivered output tokens per hour for a fixed input/output and cache mix. Let $v_A$ be the API charge per output token *including its associated input*, and $v_D$ the dedicated deployment's variable charge per output token. Let $F_D$ be its complete hourly fixed cost, including provisioned idle and reserve capacity, amortized operations, and other costs that differ between the alternatives. In a scenario with no API fixed fee, hourly costs are $qv_A$ and $F_D+qv_D$. Common costs cancel only if they are genuinely unchanged. A differing tool, verification, networking, or support cost belongs in the comparison.

If $R$ is a measured feasible output rate in tokens per second for this mix and latency target, define $u=q/(3600R)$ as a fraction of that reference hourly capacity, not GPU busy time. When $v_A>v_D$, the cost crossing is

$$u^* = \frac{F_D}{3600R(v_A-v_D)}.$$ {#eq-vol3-breakeven-utilization}

If $u^*>1$, the dedicated alternative cannot reach the crossing within the stated capacity; if $v_A\le v_D$ and $F_D>0$, it never becomes cheaper in this model. A positive crossing is a cost comparison, not evidence that the corresponding traffic satisfies deadlines or provider quotas.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-agent-economics-breakeven
#| echo: false
from mlsysim import *

class DedicatedBreakEven:
    # 1. LOAD: hypothetical matched-capability comparison; dollars and
    # token counts are scalar accounting units, time remains a quantity.
    input_per_output = 5.0
    cached_share = 0.80
    input_per_million, cached_per_million, output_per_million = 3.0, 0.30, 15.0
    fixed_per_hour = 28.0
    variable_per_million = 2.0
    reference_rate = 1_200 / second
    load_fraction = 0.52

    # 2. EXECUTE
    weighted_input = (1 - cached_share) * input_per_million + cached_share * cached_per_million
    api_per_million = output_per_million + input_per_output * weighted_input
    reference_hour_tokens = (reference_rate * hour).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    delivered_hour_tokens = load_fraction * reference_hour_tokens
    api_hour = delivered_hour_tokens * api_per_million / 1_000_000
    dedicated_hour = fixed_per_hour + delivered_hour_tokens * variable_per_million / 1_000_000
    contribution_hour = reference_hour_tokens * (api_per_million - variable_per_million) / 1_000_000
    crossing = fixed_per_hour / contribution_hour
    saving_hour = api_hour - dedicated_hour

    # 3. GUARD
    check(0 <= cached_share <= 1 and 0 < load_fraction <= 1, "Valid mix and load")
    check(reference_rate > 0 / second and fixed_per_hour > 0, "Positive capacity and commitment")
    check(
        input_per_output >= 0 and min(input_per_million, cached_per_million, output_per_million, variable_per_million) >= 0,
        "Nonnegative prices and mix",
    )
    check(api_per_million > variable_per_million and 0 < crossing < load_fraction, "This scenario crosses below its operating load")
    check(saving_hour > 0, "Dedicated cost is lower at the assumed load")

    # 4. OUTPUT
    input_per_output_str = fmt(input_per_output, precision=0)
    cached_share_str = fmt_percent(cached_share, precision=0, style="prose")
    input_price_str = fmt_usd(input_per_million, precision=0)
    cached_price_str = fmt_usd(cached_per_million, precision=1)
    output_price_str = fmt_usd(output_per_million, precision=0)
    fixed_str = fmt_usd(fixed_per_hour, precision=0)
    variable_str = fmt_usd(variable_per_million, precision=0)
    rate_str = fmt_rate(reference_rate.to(1 / second).magnitude, "tokens/s", precision=0, commas=True)
    load_str = fmt_percent(load_fraction, precision=0, style="prose")
    weighted_input_str = fmt_usd(weighted_input, precision=2)
    api_price_str = fmt_usd(api_per_million, precision=1)
    crossing_str = fmt_percent(crossing, precision=1, style="prose")
    delivered_str = fmt_int(round(delivered_hour_tokens))
    api_hour_str = fmt_usd(api_hour, precision=2)
    dedicated_hour_str = fmt_usd(dedicated_hour, precision=2)
    saving_str = fmt_usd(saving_hour, precision=2)
```

::: {#nbk-18-financial-break-even-utilization-for-dedicated .callout-notebook title="Pricing idle capacity and cached input"}

**Problem**: Assume a hypothetical matched-capability workload uses `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.input_per_output_str` input tokens per output token, with `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.cached_share_str` of inputs billed at the cached rate. API prices per million tokens are `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.input_price_str` for uncached input, `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.cached_price_str` for cached input, and `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.output_price_str` for output. A dedicated deployment costs `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.fixed_str` per hour for its entire provisioned capacity and operations, plus `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.variable_str` per million output tokens for all remaining differential variable costs.
